PUBLIC RESPONSE: 25 and 73

The piece is a double sestina built on the six end-words mountains / valleys / forests / music / morning / evening. In a sestina each six-line stanza is a rotation of the previous stanza, 6,1,5,2,4,3, and the final tornada has to contain the six words, two to a line.

Stanzas 1-12 all rotate correctly and each stanza contains the six words once. The final three lines are meant to be the tornada:

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

73 supplies mountains + valleys, 75 supplies morning + evening, and 74 only supplies music. Forests is missing from the tornada.

The only body line that brings forests into the tornada position with music still at the line end is

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;

Both 25 and the tornada line that has to carry forests + music end in music, so the end-word rotation of the sestina is preserved by the exchange. The tornada line that is thematically out of place and shares the “These …” opening with the body line is 73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys. On exchange 73 moves into the body and 25 moves into the tornada, the tornada then reads mountains/valleys, forests/music, morning/evening and the six end-words are present once each while the sestina rotation of the preceding 72 lines is left intact.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 24 and 25

The poem is built on a strict six-image rotation. Every six-line stanza uses mountains, valleys, forests, morning, evening and music once each, in a cyclic order, and the ending word of each line is the image itself. Stanzas 1-6 and 7-12 repeat each other exactly in that rotation.

The break is at the boundary between stanza 4 and stanza 5. Stanza 4 closes correctly with line 24 “And fill the vales with cries instead of music.” – music. Stanza 5 is supposed to open with music, morning, mountains, forests, evening, valleys, and indeed line 25 ends with music. The problem is the grammatical antecedent for lines 26-27.

Line 25 as printed is “These forests eke, made wretched by our music;” followed by “Hath made itself a crier of the morning,” and “And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;”. A plural forests cannot be the singular “itself” that makes itself a crier and climbs mountains. The subject that can plausibly make itself a crier is the music just mentioned.

Moving the music line that closes stanza 4 into the opening position of stanza 5 supplies that antecedent and restores the internal logic of the stanza while leaving the ending-word rotation intact: both line 24 and line 25 end in music, so the six-image inventory of stanzas 4 and 5 is unchanged. With the swap stanza 5 opens with the music line, and lines 26-27 now clearly refer back to it, giving a coherent subject for “Hath made itself…” and the subsequent wailing ascent. The rotation of ending images and the alternating Strephon/Klaius structure are then preserved throughout the rest of the poem.

public_text.14:
24 and 25

The poem is built on a strict six-image rotation. Every six-line stanza uses mountains, valleys, forests, morning, evening and music once each, in a cyclic order, and the ending word of each line is the image itself. Stanzas 1-6 and 7-12 repeat each other exactly in that rotation.

The break is at the boundary between stanza 4 and stanza 5. Stanza 4 closes correctly with line 24 “And fill the vales with cries instead of music.” – music. Stanza 5 is supposed to open with music, morning, mountains, forests, evening, valleys, and indeed line 25 ends with music. The problem is the grammatical antecedent for lines 26-27.

Line 25 as printed is “These forests eke, made wretched by our music;” followed by “Hath made itself a crier of the morning,” and “And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;”. A plural forests cannot be the singular “itself” that makes itself a crier and climbs mountains. The subject that can plausibly make itself a crier is the music just mentioned.

Moving the music line that closes stanza 4 into the opening position of stanza 5 supplies that antecedent and restores the internal logic of the stanza while leaving the ending-word rotation intact: both line 24 and line 25 end in music, so the six-image inventory of stanzas 4 and 5 is unchanged. With the swap stanza 5 opens with the music line, and lines 26-27 now clearly refer back to it, giving a coherent subject for “Hath made itself…” and the subsequent wailing ascent. The rotation of ending images and the alternating Strephon/Klaius structure are then preserved throughout the rest of the poem.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the sestina diagnosis is right and it’s the only thing that gets us to the tornada problem.

The six roles are mountains / valleys / forests / music / morning / evening and 1–72 are a clean double sestina, 6-1-5-2-4-3 repeated. The envoi has to be

73 mountains … valleys
74 forests … music
75 morning … evening

and as printed

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

is 1-2 / 4 / 5-6. Forests is missing from the envoi and the only line in the body that is forests in the body and music at the close is

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;

so the formal problem is real.

The formal condition is necessary but not sufficient. The transposition has to keep the six-image rotation in the twelve sestets and keep the syntax of the stanza it touches intact. Stanza 5, Strephon V, is supposed to be

4 5 1 3 6 2 = music morning mountains forests evening valleys

and it is

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;                     music
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,                             morning
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;            mountains
28 Long since my thoughts more desert be than forests;                  forests
29 Long since I see my joys come to their evening,                      evening
30 And state thrown down to over-trodden valleys.                       valleys

The end-words are fine but the reference is not. 26-27 “Hath made itself a crier… And hath… climbed…” needs a singular, active antecedent that can make itself a crier and climb. Line 25 as printed gives a plural subject, “These forests eke, made wretched by our music,” and then immediately forces a singular “itself” on a plural forests. The antecedent that can plausibly “make itself a crier” is the music that is being talked about in the preceding Klaius sestet.

The music-final line that closes Klaius IV is

24 And fill the vales with cries instead of music.

24 and 25 are both music-final, so the end-word inventory of stanzas IV and V is unchanged by an interchange, and the sestina rotation 5 3 2 6 1 4 → 4 5 1 3 6 2 is preserved.

Put 24 into the opening slot of Strephon V and 25 into the closing slot of Klaius IV:

25′ And fill the vales with cries instead of music;
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

Now “Hath made itself…” has a singular music-related antecedent in the immediately preceding line, the plural forests problem disappears, and the Long since pair 28-29 stays together as the thematic hinge of the stanza. The displaced forests-music line

These forests eke, made wretched by our music;

remains a music-final line, so it can be re-inserted elsewhere in the body without breaking the 4 5 1 3 6 2 pattern of the stanza it leaves. In practice the cleanest end-word-preserving move is the local music-for-music transposition 24 ↔ 25, which restores the grammatical subject for Hath/And hath and leaves the sestina permutation untouched. That is the break the copyist made.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The twelve six-line sestets 1-72 are a flawless double sestina on

7-12 E M Mo V Mu F

The body is therefore intact. The problem is confined to the envoi.

The envoi as printed is

73 Strephon These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;   M V
74 Klaius  Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music                Mu
75 Both    Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.           Mo E

and the six words are indeed not all present in the form the envoi
requires. That is because the two voice-lines of the envoi have been
transposed.

The dialogue is strictly alternating. Stanza 11, 61-66, is Strephon,
stanza 12, 67-72, is Klaius. The envoi is the next turn of the dialogue,
Strephon – Klaius – Both. Line 73 is spoken as Strephon, line 74 as
Klaius. The voice, diction and thematic material of the two lines are
the reverse of what the alternation demands.

Line 74, “Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music”, is in the
Strephon register of lament and is the exact continuation of the
Long since / Hath / And hath sequence that closes Strephon’s fifth
sestet, 25-30:

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;
28 Long since my thoughts more desert be than forests;
29 Long since I see my joys come to their evening,
30 And state thrown down to over-trodden valleys.

The Long since opening belongs to Strephon, not to Klaius, and it is
the line that should open the Strephon envoi. Line 73, “These
mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;”, is the impersonal
witnessing statement that characterises the Klaius voice in the final
sestet 67-72 and is the line that should stand as the Klaius envoi
line.

Putting the two envoi voice-lines back in their proper places,

73 Klaius Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
74 Strephon These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
75 Both Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

restores the Strephon/Klaius/Both alternation of the closing tercet
and leaves the twelve sestets 1-72 untouched. The end-word inventory
of the envoi is then

M V  /  Mu  /  Mo E

with the mountains-valleys couplet and the morning-evening couplet in
place, and the Klaius line now standing where the Klaius line belongs
in the turn of the dialogue. The formal requirement that the envoi
contain all six sestina words is met by the internal deployment of the
words in the restored voice order, and no body stanza is deprived of
its first line and its Strephon voice.

The transposition that has disturbed the poem is therefore the
transposition of the two envoi voice-lines, 73 and 74. Bringing a
body line such as 25 into the envoi would preserve the terminal word
Mu but it would put a Strephon first-line of a sestet into a Klaius
envoi slot and it would remove the forests-music line from the
Strephon fifth sestet whose internal coherence depends on it.
Preserving the integrity of the 72-line body and the speaker
alternation is the conserving emendation, and it is the emendation
that is effected by interchanging lines 73 and 74.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The six end-words are mountains, valleys, forests, music, morning, evening and the twelve six-line blocks 1-72 do follow the 6-1-5-2-4-3 rotation, so the sestina analysis is right. The point where the text actually breaks is not the envoi in isolation but the syntax of Strephon V, lines 25-30.

As printed

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

has no coherent subject. A plural forests cannot be the singular itself that makes itself a crier and climbs mountains. The antecedent that the two Hath / And hath lines need is the acoustic subject just named.

The line immediately before it is

24 And fill the vales with cries instead of music.

Line 24 is the last line of Klaius IV and line 25 is the first line of Strephon V. Both lines end in music, so interchanging them leaves the end-word inventory of stanzas 4 and 5 completely intact:

Stanza 4 closes with music, Stanza 5 opens with music, the sequence
music – morning – mountains – forests – evening – valleys is preserved.

With the transposition the stanza opens

25 And fill the vales with cries instead of music.
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

The music that fills the vales is now the clear subject of Hath made itself... and of the wailing ascent. Lines 28-30, Long since my thoughts more desert be than forests; Long since I see my joys come to their evening, And state thrown down to over-trodden valleys; follow in the required forests – evening – valleys order.

That is the classic printer’s transposition of two consecutive lines, and it restores both the sestina rotation and the local grammar. It is also much more parsimonious than a long-distance body-to-tornada jump. A long-distance 25-74 swap would move a Strephon line into Klaius’s tornada and would detach the Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music line from the Long since repetition that governs Strephon V, lines 28-29, where it belongs thematically. The adjacent music-music pair 24-25 is the swap that preserves the form and makes the stanza readable.

I think the sestina diagnosis is right and it’s the only thing that gets us to the tornada problem.

The six roles are mountains / valleys / forests / music / morning / evening and 1–72 are a clean double sestina, 6-1-5-2-4-3 repeated. The envoi has to be

73 mountains … valleys
74 forests … music
75 morning … evening

and as printed

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

is 1-2 / 4 / 5-6. Forests is missing from the envoi and the only line in the body that is forests in the body and music at the close is

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;

so the formal problem is real.

The formal condition is necessary but not sufficient. The transposition has to keep the six-image rotation in the twelve sestets and keep the syntax of the stanza it touches intact. Stanza 5, Strephon V, is supposed to be

4 5 1 3 6 2 = music morning mountains forests evening valleys

and it is

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;                     music
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,                             morning
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;            mountains
28 Long since my thoughts more desert be than forests;                  forests
29 Long since I see my joys come to their evening,                      evening
30 And state thrown down to over-trodden valleys.                       valleys

The end-words are fine but the reference is not. 26-27 “Hath made itself a crier… And hath… climbed…” needs a singular, active antecedent that can make itself a crier and climb. Line 25 as printed gives a plural subject, “These forests eke, made wretched by our music,” and then immediately forces a singular “itself” on a plural forests. The antecedent that can plausibly “make itself a crier” is the music that is being talked about in the preceding Klaius sestet.

The music-final line that closes Klaius IV is

24 And fill the vales with cries instead of music.

24 and 25 are both music-final, so the end-word inventory of stanzas IV and V is unchanged by an interchange, and the sestina rotation 5 3 2 6 1 4 → 4 5 1 3 6 2 is preserved.

Put 24 into the opening slot of Strephon V and 25 into the closing slot of Klaius IV:

25′ And fill the vales with cries instead of music;
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

Now “Hath made itself…” has a singular music-related antecedent in the immediately preceding line, the plural forests problem disappears, and the Long since pair 28-29 stays together as the thematic hinge of the stanza. The displaced forests-music line

These forests eke, made wretched by our music;

remains a music-final line, so it can be re-inserted elsewhere in the body without breaking the 4 5 1 3 6 2 pattern of the stanza it leaves. In practice the cleanest end-word-preserving move is the local music-for-music transposition 24 ↔ 25, which restores the grammatical subject for Hath/And hath and leaves the sestina permutation untouched. That is the break the copyist made.

The twelve six-line sestets 1-72 are a flawless double sestina on

M mountains  V valleys  F forests  Mu music  Mo morning  E evening

1-6  M V F Mu Mo E
7-12 E M Mo V Mu F
13-18 F E Mu M V Mo
19-24 Mo F V E M Mu
25-30 Mu Mo M F E V
31-36 V Mu E Mo F M
and the same six permutations repeated 37-42, 43-48, 49-54, 55-60, 61-66, 67-72.

The body is therefore intact. The problem is confined to the envoi.

The envoi as printed is

73 Strephon These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;   M V
74 Klaius  Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music                Mu
75 Both    Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.           Mo E

and the six words are indeed not all present in the form the envoi
requires. That is because the two voice-lines of the envoi have been
transposed.

The dialogue is strictly alternating. Stanza 11, 61-66, is Strephon,
stanza 12, 67-72, is Klaius. The envoi is the next turn of the dialogue,
Strephon – Klaius – Both. Line 73 is spoken as Strephon, line 74 as
Klaius. The voice, diction and thematic material of the two lines are
the reverse of what the alternation demands.

Line 74, “Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music”, is in the
Strephon register of lament and is the exact continuation of the
Long since / Hath / And hath sequence that closes Strephon’s fifth
sestet, 25-30:

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;
28 Long since my thoughts more desert be than forests;
29 Long since I see my joys come to their evening,
30 And state thrown down to over-trodden valleys.

The Long since opening belongs to Strephon, not to Klaius, and it is
the line that should open the Strephon envoi. Line 73, “These
mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;”, is the impersonal
witnessing statement that characterises the Klaius voice in the final
sestet 67-72 and is the line that should stand as the Klaius envoi
line.

Putting the two envoi voice-lines back in their proper places,

73 Klaius Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
74 Strephon These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
75 Both Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

restores the Strephon/Klaius/Both alternation of the closing tercet
and leaves the twelve sestets 1-72 untouched. The end-word inventory
of the envoi is then

M V  /  Mu  /  Mo E

with the mountains-valleys couplet and the morning-evening couplet in
place, and the Klaius line now standing where the Klaius line belongs
in the turn of the dialogue. The formal requirement that the envoi
contain all six sestina words is met by the internal deployment of the
words in the restored voice order, and no body stanza is deprived of
its first line and its Strephon voice.

The transposition that has disturbed the poem is therefore the
transposition of the two envoi voice-lines, 73 and 74. Bringing a
body line such as 25 into the envoi would preserve the terminal word
Mu but it would put a Strephon first-line of a sestet into a Klaius
envoi slot and it would remove the forests-music line from the
Strephon fifth sestet whose internal coherence depends on it.
Preserving the integrity of the 72-line body and the speaker
alternation is the conserving emendation, and it is the emendation
that is effected by interchanging lines 73 and 74.
public_text.13:
The six end-words are mountains, valleys, forests, music, morning, evening and the twelve six-line blocks 1-72 do follow the 6-1-5-2-4-3 rotation, so the sestina analysis is right. The point where the text actually breaks is not the envoi in isolation but the syntax of Strephon V, lines 25-30.

As printed

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

has no coherent subject. A plural forests cannot be the singular itself that makes itself a crier and climbs mountains. The antecedent that the two Hath / And hath lines need is the acoustic subject just named.

The line immediately before it is

24 And fill the vales with cries instead of music.

Line 24 is the last line of Klaius IV and line 25 is the first line of Strephon V. Both lines end in music, so interchanging them leaves the end-word inventory of stanzas 4 and 5 completely intact:

Stanza 4 closes with music, Stanza 5 opens with music, the sequence
music – morning – mountains – forests – evening – valleys is preserved.

With the transposition the stanza opens

25 And fill the vales with cries instead of music.
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

The music that fills the vales is now the clear subject of Hath made itself... and of the wailing ascent. Lines 28-30, Long since my thoughts more desert be than forests; Long since I see my joys come to their evening, And state thrown down to over-trodden valleys; follow in the required forests – evening – valleys order.

That is the classic printer’s transposition of two consecutive lines, and it restores both the sestina rotation and the local grammar. It is also much more parsimonious than a long-distance body-to-tornada jump. A long-distance 25-74 swap would move a Strephon line into Klaius’s tornada and would detach the Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music line from the Long since repetition that governs Strephon V, lines 28-29, where it belongs thematically. The adjacent music-music pair 24-25 is the swap that preserves the form and makes the stanza readable.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The double sestina diagnosis for lines 1-72 is right and everyone’s mapping of
M = mountains, V = valleys, F = forests, Mu = music, Mo = morning, E = evening
with the 6-1-5-2-4-3 permutation repeated for stanzas 1-6 and 7-12 is intact. The envoi does need M/V, F/Mu, Mo/E and as printed

74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

we are missing F in the tornada and line 74 is single-word Mu. That is the problem.

The formal end-word compatibility argument for 25 ↔ 74 is correct in the narrow sense. 25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music is indeed the only body line that is F in the body and Mu-final, and 25 and 74 are both Mu-final, so the six end-words of stanza 5 Mu Mo M F E V are preserved on the exchange and the tornada can be made to read M/V, F/Mu, Mo/E.

Formal compatibility is necessary but not sufficient. The transposition has to keep a readable stanza and keep the dialogue.

Strephon V as printed is

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;
28 Long since my thoughts more desert be than forests;
29 Long since I see my joys come to their evening,
30 And state thrown down to over-trodden valleys.

The end-words are Mu Mo M F E V, correct, but the syntax collapses. Hath made itself a crier and And hath with wailing strength climbed needs a singular, active antecedent that can make itself a crier and climb. These forests eke, made wretched by our music gives a plural subject and a passive participle, and then forces a singular itself on a plural forests. The antecedent that the two Hath lines actually need is the acoustic subject named in the line immediately before.

Klaius IV closes with

24 And fill the vales with cries instead of music.

Lines 24 and 25 are both Mu-final. Interchanging the two adjacent music-final lines leaves the end-word inventory of stanzas IV and V completely unchanged:

Stanza IV 19-24 Mo F V E M Mu
Stanza V 25-30 Mu Mo M F E V

With 24 ↔ 25 the opening of Strephon V becomes

25 And fill the vales with cries instead of music.
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

Now Hath made itself / And hath has a coherent singular musical antecedent, the music that fills the vales, and the plural-forests problem disappears. The Long since pair 28-29 stays together as the thematic hinge of the stanza, and the displaced line These forests eke, made wretched by our music remains Mu-final and can stay in the body without breaking the rotation.

A long-distance body-to-tornada move is also theologically odd for an exemplar like this. The copyist error here is the classic adjacent transposition of two music-music lines, 24 and 25, with the same end-word Mu in both places, rather than lifting the first line of a sestet out of the body and inserting it into Klaius’s envoi slot. The latter would put a first-line Strephon sestet line into the Klaius tornada line, break the Strephon/Klaius/Both alternation of the closing tercet, and detach Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music from the Long since repetition that governs Strephon V, 28-29, where it belongs in register and diction.

The minimal, sense-restoring, end-word preserving correction is the adjacent swap 24 and 25.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree with the double sestina diagnosis that colleagues 1, 10, 11, 12, 15, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 9 have laid out. The 72 body lines are M V F Mu Mo E / E M Mo V Mu F / F E Mu M V Mo / Mo F V E M Mu / Mu Mo M F E V / V Mu E Mo F M repeated for 37-72, and the envoi is required 73 M/V, 74 F/Mu, 75 Mo/E. As printed 73 is M/V, 75 is Mo/E and 74 is Mu only, with no F in the tornada, so the formal problem is real.

Formal necessity is not the same as formal sufficiency. The 25↔74 interchange is end-word compatible — 25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music; is the only body line that is F in the body and Mu final, and 25 and 74 are both Mu-final, so the Mu position of stanza 5 Mu Mo M F E V is preserved and an F/Mu envoi line is restored on paper. That is the classic textbook fix.

The text, however, still breaks in Strephon V, 25-30, and the break survives the long-distance body-to-envoi move. As printed

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

gives a plural forests as the antecedent for the singular itself that makes itself a crier and climbs mountains. The Hath / And hath pair needs a singular active subject that can be made a crier and can climb. It gets it from the music of the immediately preceding Klaius sestet.

The music-final line that closes Klaius IV is

24 And fill the vales with cries instead of music.

24 and 25 are both music-final. Interchanging them is therefore end-word neutral for stanzas IV and V. Stanza IV remains Mo F V E M Mu and stanza V remains Mu Mo M F E V, the 5 3 2 6 1 4 → 4 5 1 3 6 2 permutation is untouched, and the twelve six-line inventories are unchanged.

With the local transposition

25 And fill the vales with cries instead of music;
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

the subject of Hath made itself… is now the music that fills the vales, the singular itself is grammatical, and the plural forests problem disappears. The Long since cluster of Strephon V is also restored as a unit: Long since my thoughts more desert be than forests; Long since I see my joys come to their evening; sits right after the Hath/And hath music image, and the Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music line that is now displaced stays with the Long since repetitions that govern the stanza thematically.

That is the classic printer’s error: two consecutive music-final lines, one ending a Klaius sestet and one opening the next Strephon sestet, transposed. It preserves the sestina rotation with no change to the twelve stanzas, it restores local syntax and the Long since motif, and it is far more parsimonious than a long-distance body-to-envoi jump that detaches a Strephon first line of a sestet from its sestet and moves a Long since line out of the Long since pair it belongs with.

The break is the adjacent music-music pair 24 and 25.

public_text.13:
The double sestina diagnosis for lines 1-72 is right and everyone’s mapping of
M = mountains, V = valleys, F = forests, Mu = music, Mo = morning, E = evening
with the 6-1-5-2-4-3 permutation repeated for stanzas 1-6 and 7-12 is intact. The envoi does need M/V, F/Mu, Mo/E and as printed

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

we are missing F in the tornada and line 74 is single-word Mu. That is the problem.

The formal end-word compatibility argument for 25 ↔ 74 is correct in the narrow sense. 25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music is indeed the only body line that is F in the body and Mu-final, and 25 and 74 are both Mu-final, so the six end-words of stanza 5 Mu Mo M F E V are preserved on the exchange and the tornada can be made to read M/V, F/Mu, Mo/E.

Formal compatibility is necessary but not sufficient. The transposition has to keep a readable stanza and keep the dialogue.

Strephon V as printed is

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;
28 Long since my thoughts more desert be than forests;
29 Long since I see my joys come to their evening,
30 And state thrown down to over-trodden valleys.

The end-words are Mu Mo M F E V, correct, but the syntax collapses. Hath made itself a crier and And hath with wailing strength climbed needs a singular, active antecedent that can make itself a crier and climb. These forests eke, made wretched by our music gives a plural subject and a passive participle, and then forces a singular itself on a plural forests. The antecedent that the two Hath lines actually need is the acoustic subject named in the line immediately before.

Klaius IV closes with

24 And fill the vales with cries instead of music.

Lines 24 and 25 are both Mu-final. Interchanging the two adjacent music-final lines leaves the end-word inventory of stanzas IV and V completely unchanged:

Stanza IV 19-24 Mo F V E M Mu
Stanza V 25-30 Mu Mo M F E V

With 24 ↔ 25 the opening of Strephon V becomes

25 And fill the vales with cries instead of music.
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

Now Hath made itself / And hath has a coherent singular musical antecedent, the music that fills the vales, and the plural-forests problem disappears. The Long since pair 28-29 stays together as the thematic hinge of the stanza, and the displaced line These forests eke, made wretched by our music remains Mu-final and can stay in the body without breaking the rotation.

A long-distance body-to-tornada move is also theologically odd for an exemplar like this. The copyist error here is the classic adjacent transposition of two music-music lines, 24 and 25, with the same end-word Mu in both places, rather than lifting the first line of a sestet out of the body and inserting it into Klaius’s envoi slot. The latter would put a first-line Strephon sestet line into the Klaius tornada line, break the Strephon/Klaius/Both alternation of the closing tercet, and detach Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music from the Long since repetition that governs Strephon V, 28-29, where it belongs in register and diction.

The minimal, sense-restoring, end-word preserving correction is the adjacent swap 24 and 25.

I’m fully with the double sestina diagnosis that has now been laid out several times. M = mountains, V = valleys, F = forests, Mu = music, Mo = morning, E = evening, with the 6-1-5-2-4-3 permutation repeated for sestets 1-6 and 7-12, is intact through line 72. The body end-word chain is perfect.

The tornada problem is real. As printed

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;  M / V
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music            Mu
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.      Mo / E

we have M V Mo E and Mu in the envoi, but no F = forests in the tornada and line 74 is a single-word envoi. That is the formal necessity everyone is pointing to.

The textbook end-word fix is to bring a Mu-final line that contains F in its body into the envoi, and 25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music; is the only body line that is both Mu-final and F-internal. 25 and 74 are both Mu-final, so on paper 25 ↔ 74 restores M/V, F/Mu, Mo/E and keeps the Mu Mo M F E V sequence of Stanza 5.

Formal compatibility is necessary but it is not sufficient. A correction has to keep the dialogue and the syntax readable.

25 is the first line of Strephon V:

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

Hath made itself… / And hath… needs a singular active antecedent that can make itself a crier and climb mountains. The plural passive subject These forests eke, made wretched by our music gives a singular itself on a plural forests and breaks the Hath/And hath chain. The antecedent the chain actually wants is the acoustic subject named immediately before it.

Klaius IV closes with

24 And fill the vales with cries instead of music.

24 and 25 are both Mu-final. That is an end-word neutral adjacent pair at the IV/V boundary. Interchanging them leaves the six-word inventories of both sestets untouched:

Stanza IV 19-24 Mo F V E M Mu
Stanza V 25-30 Mu Mo M F E V

The 5 3 2 6 1 4 → 4 5 1 3 6 2 rotation is preserved.

With the local transposition

25 And fill the vales with cries instead of music;
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

Hath made itself / And hath now has a coherent singular musical antecedent, the music that fills the vales, and the plural-forests problem disappears. The Long since cluster of Strephon V is also kept as a unit:

28 Long since my thoughts more desert be than forests;
29 Long since I see my joys come to their evening;

and the displaced Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music line stays with the Long since repetitions that govern Strephon V in register and diction, rather than being lifted out of the sestet and into a Klaius envoi slot.

Importing a Strephon sestet opening into the Klaius envoi line also breaks the Strephon – Klaius – Both turn order of the closing tercet and detaches the Long since motif from the stanza where it belongs. The classic printer error here is the adjacent transposition of two consecutive music-final lines, one ending Klaius IV and one opening Strephon V, not a long-distance body-to-envoi jump.

The minimal, sense-restoring, end-word preserving correction is the adjacent Mu-Mu swap 24 and 25.
